paras: The disappearance of George Washington in posse custody took place in Catahoula Parish, Louisiana, in or before early May 1888, when a Black boy accused of killing a white farmer was captured by a constable and posse and never brought to Harrisonburg. Two Louisiana papers supposed that he had been killed on the way, one suggesting a hanging, but neither reported his death as fact.

According to the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe, W. H. Taylor, a white citizen of Catahoula Parish, was waylaid, shot and killed while plowing in his field. The accused was George Washington, described as "a negro boy" of about 17 years who had a wooden leg.

The St. Landry Democrat said the boy fled after the killing and was captured by a posse. Quoting the Harrisonburg News, the Telegraph reported that the constable of the ward and a posse had started for Harrisonburg with him but had not arrived, and that "it is conjectured that he might have escaped from the posse."

The coverage shows no later sighting of the boy and no inquest, arrest or official inquiry. By late May the Democrat wrote that because "some time has elapsed since the capture" without his appearance, he was "supposed" to have been hanged.

The story appeared only in brief items in the Ouachita Telegraph on May 12 and the St. Landry Democrat on May 26, 1888. The Telegraph read the News's talk of escape as a euphemism, writing that neither the boy's wooden leg "nor the distinction of passing under the name of the Father of his Country saved him." It added that he "probably escaped a trial by jury," but that the crime was "a horrible one" and his fate "well merited" if he got "lost" in the woods. The Democrat treated the supposed hanging as a joke, saying he had lost his life "trying to kick the filling out of a hemp rope."
The Harrisonburg News, as quoted, offered escape as the explanation for the boy's absence; the Democrat supposed a hanging, and the Telegraph implied a killing without naming a method.

reader.title: Disappearance of George Washington in posse custody
bases: Both papers report that a Black boy accused of murder was captured by a constable and posse and never brought in, and both suppose he was put to death (A1, A2).

Neither paper confirms a death: the Telegraph says he 'probably escaped a trial by jury' and the Democrat says 'it is supposed' he was hanged, but both rest on his failure to arrive at Harrisonburg (A1, A2). Any killing would have been without trial and in answer to a murder accusation, but the posse's size is not given.
Only two short items exist and neither reports the boy's death as fact; the Democrat's version adds a supposed hanging but cites no source beyond the boy's non-appearance (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Harrisonburg News (local, quoted)
accounts.gist: The constable and a posse captured the boy and started for Harrisonburg but had not arrived; with bad roads and thick woods, 'it is conjectured' he escaped from the posse.

accounts.label: Ouachita Telegraph comment
accounts.gist: Read the News item as meaning the boy was killed: neither his wooden leg nor his name 'saved him', and he 'probably escaped a trial by jury'.

accounts.label: St. Landry Democrat
accounts.gist: The boy escaped, was captured by a posse, and since he had not appeared it was 'supposed' he had been hanged.

framing.detail: The Telegraph called the killing of Taylor 'a horrible one' and said that if the boy got 'lost' in the woods 'his fate was well merited'.
The Democrat made a joke of a supposed hanging: he 'lost his life trying to kick the filling out of a hemp rope'.
